opus-5.5.text:
I think simulation-centered companies will become something like the infrastructure layer of robotics, but probably not in the way people imagined a few years ago.

Early on, there was this hope that you could build a perfect digital twin of the world, train everything in simulation, and then just deploy to real robots with zero real-world data. In practice, the sim-to-real gap turned out to be stubborn, especially for contact-rich manipulation: deformable objects, friction, cables, cloth, liquids. Physics engines are very good at rigid bodies and locomotion, which is why legged robots benefited so much from simulation. But for dexterous hands working in a messy kitchen, simulation alone hasn't been enough.

So where does that leave simulation companies? I see three roles.

First, simulation as a data multiplier rather than a data replacement. You collect a relatively small amount of real teleoperation data, and then use simulation, plus increasingly generative models, to expand it: randomizing scenes, lighting, object poses, embodiments. The real data anchors you to reality, and the synthetic data gives you coverage.

Second, simulation as evaluation infrastructure. This is underrated. As robot foundation models get bigger, the bottleneck shifts from "can we train it" to "how do we know it's better." Real-world evaluation is slow, expensive, and hard to reproduce. If you can build simulated benchmarks that actually correlate with real-world performance, that's enormously valuable. Whoever owns trusted evaluation will have real influence over the whole ecosystem.

Third, and I think most interesting, is the convergence between physics simulation and world models. Learned video and world models are starting to act like simulators: you give them an action and they predict what happens next. They're not physically exact, but they capture visual diversity and long-tail situations that hand-built engines never will. The winning simulation companies will probably be hybrids: physics where physics is reliable, learned models where the world is too messy to hand-code.

The risk for a pure simulation company is that it becomes a tools vendor squeezed between big model companies and hardware companies. If the large labs build their own world models internally, and the hardware makers own the real-world data flywheel, the standalone simulation player has to find a defensible position. I think that position is either owning the evaluation standard, or becoming deeply embedded in a specific vertical, like warehouses or factories, where you understand the domain well enough that your simulation is genuinely better than a generic one.

So my short answer: simulation won't be the whole story, but it'll be indispensable. The companies that survive will be the ones that stop selling simulation as a product and start selling what it enables: faster iteration, cheaper data, and trustworthy measurement.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining simulation with a small amount of real data and generative models, and separately discusses foundation models and hardware companies. It does not present that combination, including hardware supplied by hardware companies, as a route to end-to-end deployment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think simulation-centered companies are going to end up occupying a position in robotics that looks a lot like what the chip foundries or the cloud providers became for software: not the thing the end customer sees, but the layer everyone else is forced to build on.

The reason is pretty simple. The bottleneck in robotics is no longer the hardware, and it's increasingly not the model architecture either. It's data. A humanoid or a manipulation arm needs an enormous volume of experience, and collecting that in the real world is slow, expensive, and dangerous. You can't crash a hundred thousand robots into kitchen counters to learn how to open a cabinet. So the only path to the scale that these learning systems demand is to generate most of that experience synthetically, and then close the gap between simulation and reality with a comparatively small amount of real data.

That means whoever owns the simulation stack owns something very valuable: the physics fidelity, the asset libraries, the scene generation, the domain randomization tooling, and crucially the pipeline that turns all of that into a training signal. Over time I expect those companies to look less like software vendors selling a license and more like data utilities. You'll see them selling pre-trained policies, benchmark environments, even certification services, where a robot has to pass a battery of simulated scenarios before it's allowed into a warehouse or a hospital.

There are a couple of risks, though. One is that the large foundation model labs decide simulation is core and build it in-house, which squeezes the independents. Another is that the sim-to-real gap turns out to be stubborn in exactly the areas that matter most, like deformable objects, contact-rich manipulation, and anything involving humans. If that happens, the value shifts back toward companies with large real-world fleets.

My own view is that it won't be either-or. The winners will be the ones who treat simulation and real deployment as a single flywheel: real data improves the simulator, the simulator produces policies that go out into the world, and the world sends back the failure cases. Simulation companies that stay purely virtual will struggle. The ones that become the connective tissue between the virtual and physical worlds, I think, become indispensable.

r001.rationale: The response describes synthetic simulation experience combined with a comparatively small amount of real-world data, and policies deployed into the world. It does not identify foundation models and hardware supplied by hardware companies as part of a route to end-to-end deployment.

astra-6.text:
I think their role will depend on how well they connect simulation to what happens in the real world. Simulation lets you test ideas quickly, explore failures, and train systems without putting a physical robot through every experiment. But the real test is whether that work makes the robot more reliable when it leaves the simulator.

So I see these companies becoming part of the development infrastructure for robotics. The strongest ones will help teams build a continuous loop: collect data from real robots, use it to improve the simulation, train and test, then bring the results back into deployment.

There’s also a question of where they specialize. Some may provide tools across many types of robots; others may go deep into a particular task where accurately modeling contact or materials really matters. Either way, the value will be in reducing the time and cost of getting a robot to do useful work reliably.

r001.rationale: The response describes a simulation and real-robot data loop, but does not identify foundation models, a small amount of real-world data, hardware supplied by hardware companies, or that combination as a route to end-to-end deployment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think their role will grow, but the key question is whether simulation actually helps robots work better in the real world. Building a convincing virtual environment is one thing; using it to improve reliability, reduce development time, and handle unfamiliar situations is another.

The most valuable companies will probably build a tight loop between simulation and physical deployment. Real-world failures inform the simulation, and simulation lets teams test improvements before putting them back on a robot. That loop matters more than visual realism alone.

There’s also an opportunity to become shared infrastructure. Different robotics teams need ways to train, test, and compare their systems. But whether a company provides that infrastructure or builds robots itself, I’d judge it by the same outcome: how much does its simulation improve performance outside the simulator?

r001.rationale: The response describes a feedback loop between simulation and physical deployment, but does not identify combining simulation with a small amount of real-world data, foundation models, and hardware supplied by hardware companies as a route to end-to-end deployment.
